::: {.at-a-glance}
- **Time:** 80 minutes in class, together with the [lesson 03 hands-on](03-data-management.qmd), or about 60 minutes alone.
- **Slides:** [Project organization](../lectures/02-project-organization/02-project-organization.qmd)
- **You need:** [lesson 00](00-setup.qmd) done (Pixi installed), paper and a pen.
- **You will have:** the `ltee-project` folder that every later lesson builds on.
:::

## Overview

Everyone who has worked on a project for a few months knows the folder full of
`final.csv`, `final_v2.csv` and `final_USE_THIS.csv`. A good layout prevents
that. It is not one of the five pillars of computational reproducibility
(literate programming, version control, environment control, data sharing,
documentation; Ziemann et al. 2023), but each pillar is easier when files are
where everyone expects them. In this lesson you first design a layout yourself, then
compare it with published advice, then generate one from a template so you
can see every choice the template makes for you.

The running example is the **LTEE project**: variant calling on three samples
of *E. coli* from Richard Lenski's Long-Term Evolution Experiment, taken at
5,000, 15,000 and 50,000 generations. You do not need to know any genomics:
treat the analysis as a given pipeline. What matters is how the project is
organized and whether someone else can rerun it.

### Learning outcomes

After this lesson you can:

1. **Create** a new analysis project from a template with one command and say what belongs in each folder.
2. **Separate** raw data, derived data, code and results so that raw data is never modified and results can be deleted and rebuilt.
3. **Name** files so they sort correctly and can be read by people and programs.
4. **Write** scripts with paths relative to the project folder, and show why absolute paths break.

Each outcome is checked by a step below; the last one by the *Break it* exercise.

### Prerequisites

[Lesson 00](00-setup.qmd): Pixi works (`pixi --version`). Basic shell: `cd`, `ls`, `mkdir`.

## 1. Sketch first (10 minutes, on paper)

Before you look at any template, design the project yourself. You will
analyze sequencing data for three samples. The analysis needs:

- six FASTQ files (two per sample), downloaded from figshare;
- a reference genome, downloaded from NCBI;
- a table describing the samples (generation, strain, file names);
- a few scripts and, later, a Snakemake and a Nextflow pipeline;
- the software environment (Pixi files);
- outputs: quality-control reports, alignments, variant calls, plots;
- a report that explains the results;
- a README, a license and a citation file.

On paper, draw the folders you would create and put each item in one. Mark
which files you would **never edit by hand** and which you could **delete and
rebuild**.

::: {.callout-note title="Think, pair, share (5 minutes)"}
Compare your sketch with a neighbor. Where did you disagree? Which file was
hardest to place? Keep your sketch: you will compare it with the template in
step 4.
:::

## 2. What others recommend

Two short papers are the classic advice for organizing computational biology
projects. Read the key points below; the full papers are in *Further reading*.

**Noble (2009), "A quick guide to organizing computational biology projects":**

- one folder per project, with the same layout every time;
- separate folders for `data`, `src` (code), `bin` (compiled tools), `results` and `doc`;
- raw data stays as it was received; everything else is made from it by code;
- a dated lab notebook (`results/2009-01-15/`) records what you did and why;
- a "driver" script reruns the whole analysis.

**Wilson et al. (2017), "Good enough practices in scientific computing":**

- put each project in its own directory, named after the project;
- put text documents in `doc/`, raw data and metadata in `data/`, files
  generated during cleanup and analysis in `results/`, source code in `src/`;
- name all files to reflect their content or function;
- keep raw data read-only, and create the data you analyse with code.

Both agree on the main rule: **raw data in, code in the middle, results out,
and results can always be regenerated.**

## 3. Generate the project from the template

A *template* creates the same, well-thought-out layout every time, so you do
not have to remember it. We use [Cookiecutter](https://cookiecutter.readthedocs.io/),
run through Pixi, so you do not need to install it.

Create a folder for this course and go into it:

```{.bash .run}
mkdir -p ~/cbio7501
cd ~/cbio7501
```

Run the template. Cookiecutter asks a few questions; press Enter to keep the
value in brackets. Use `ltee-project` as the folder name:

```{.bash .norun}
pixi exec --spec cookiecutter --spec git -- \
  cookiecutter gh:khan-lab/cbio7501-f26 --directory templates/cookiecutter-repro-project
```

```text
  [1/12] Project name (a few words) (LTEE variant calling):
  [2/12] Folder and repository name (lowercase, dashes) (ltee-variant-calling): ltee-project
  [3/12] One sentence: what does this project do? (A reproducible analysis project): Variant calling on LTEE E. coli samples
  [4/12] Your given name(s) (Your): Ada
  ...
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Same thing, without the questions"}
You can give all answers on the command line. This is what the course tests
run; use your own name and ORCID iD:

```{.bash .run}
pixi exec --spec cookiecutter --spec git -- \
  cookiecutter --no-input gh:khan-lab/cbio7501-f26 --directory templates/cookiecutter-repro-project \
  project_name="LTEE variant calling" project_slug="ltee-project" \
  short_description="Variant calling on three E. coli samples from the Long-Term Evolution Experiment" \
  author_given_names="Ada" author_family_names="Lovelace" author_email="ada@example.org" \
  github_username="ada-lovelace" license="MIT"
```
:::

Expected output ends with:

```text
Created ltee-project/

Next steps:
  cd ltee-project
  pixi install            # create the environment and pixi.lock
  pixi run check          # check that the tools work
```

(Not now: you create the environment in [lesson 05](05-pixi.qmd).)

## 4. Walk through the layout

List the folders:

```{.bash .run}
cd ~/cbio7501/ltee-project
find . -type d | sort
```

```text
.
./.github
./.github/workflows
./config
./containers
./data
./data/processed
./data/raw
./docs
./envs
./metadata
./notebooks
./reports
./results
./scripts
./workflow
```

Every folder has a `README.md` that says what goes in it. Read two of them:

```{.bash .run}
cat data/raw/README.md
cat results/README.md
```

The main `README.md` has a table of all folders. Here is the logic in one picture:

```text
  data/raw/  ──code──►  data/processed/  ──code──►  results/  ──►  reports/
  (read-only,           (derived,                   (figures,      (Quarto
   downloaded)           rebuildable)                tables)        report)
       ▲                                                  ▲
  metadata/  (what each file is, where it came from, checksums)
  scripts/, workflow/, config/  (the code and its parameters)
  pixi.toml + pixi.lock  (the software)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Compare with your sketch (5 minutes)"}
Go through your paper sketch. For each difference, decide: is the template
better, is your version better, or is it a matter of taste? Two points worth
discussing:

- The template has **no** `final/` folder and no dated `results/2026-10-27/`
  folders (Noble's lab notebook). Results are regenerated by code; history is
  kept by Git (lesson 04).
- `metadata/` is separate from `data/`: it is small, written by people and
  committed to Git, while `data/` is large, downloaded and not committed.
:::

### What else the template created

```{.bash .run}
ls -a
cat pixi.toml
```

- `pixi.toml`: the software this project needs (Python, Quarto, Jupyter,
  pandas, matplotlib). You learn how it works in [lesson 05](05-pixi.qmd).
- `.gitignore`: tells Git ([lesson 04](04-git.qmd)) not to track raw data,
  results and the installed environment.
- `LICENSE` and `CITATION.cff`: how others may reuse and cite the project
  (lesson 11).
- `.github/workflows/reproduce.yml`: a check that reruns the project on a
  fresh computer every time you push (from lesson 04; it gets real work in
  lesson 05).

## 5. Name files so that they sort and explain themselves

A good file name is readable by people, easy for programs to parse, and sorts
in a useful order. Rules we follow in this course:

- no spaces or special characters; use `-` or `_`;
- dates as `YYYY-MM-DD` (ISO 8601), so they sort in time order;
- numbers with leading zeros (`s01`, `s02`, ..., `s12`);
- the most important part first (the sample ID, if you look files up by sample);
- the same parts in the same order in every name, with the abbreviations
  explained in `metadata/README.md`;
- a version number only for things you release (`v001`); everything else is versioned by Git.

The LTEE files follow these rules already: `SRR2584863_1.trim.sub.fastq` is
run `SRR2584863`, read 1 of the pair, trimmed, subsampled.

### Try it yourself

1. These names were sorted alphabetically by a computer. What problems do
   you see?

   ```text
   12-10-2026 alignment SRR2589044.bam
   2026-10-13_SRR2584866_aligned.bam
   2026-10-9_SRR2584863_aligned.bam
   Final results (use this).xlsx
   SRR2584863_aligned_v2.bam
   sample1.bam
   sample10.bam
   sample2.bam
   ```

   ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
   - Two date formats; `12-10-2026` is ambiguous (December or October?) and does not sort.
   - `2026-10-9` lacks a leading zero, so it sorts *after* `2026-10-13`.
   - Spaces and brackets break shell commands unless quoted.
   - `sample10` sorts between `sample1` and `sample2` (no leading zeros).
   - `_v2` and "use this" are manual version control; use Git instead.
   - The sample ID moves around, so you cannot list all files of a sample with one pattern.

   A consistent version: `SRR2584863.aligned.sorted.bam`, `SRR2584866.aligned.sorted.bam`,
   `SRR2589044.aligned.sorted.bam`, made by code in `results/bam/`.
   :::

2. Which name in each group follows the rules best?

   a) `variant counts 5Aug2026.csv` b) `variant-counts_2026-08-05.csv` c) `counts.csv`

   ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
   b): no spaces, ISO date, says what is inside. c) is too vague; a) has spaces
   and a date that does not sort.
   :::

## 6. Start the README now

A README written on day one is a plan; one written at the end is a chore. Open
`README.md` in your editor and fill in the *Data* section. You can copy this:

```markdown
## Data

Raw reads: a subset (175,000 read pairs per sample) of three *E. coli* clones
from the Long-Term Evolution Experiment (population Ara-3, generations 5,000,
15,000 and 50,000), prepared by Data Carpentry:
<https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.7726454> (file `sub.tar.gz`, CC0).
Reference genome: *E. coli* B str. REL606, GenBank CP000819.1 (NCBI).
Details, sample sheet and checksums are in `metadata/`.
```

You will download the data and write the sample sheet in the
[lesson 03 hands-on](03-data-management.qmd#hands-on).

## Break it: absolute paths

A script that only works in one folder on one laptop is not reproducible. See
it fail. First write a tiny script that reads a file through an **absolute**
path (the full path on *your* computer, which the shell fills in with `$PWD`):

```{.bash .run}
cd ~/cbio7501/ltee-project
echo "print(open('$PWD/metadata/README.md').readline())" > scripts/first_line_absolute.py
cat scripts/first_line_absolute.py
pixi exec python scripts/first_line_absolute.py
```

It works. Now do what a colleague does when they download your project: put
it in a different folder. Here we just rename the project folder:

```{.bash .run}
cd ~/cbio7501
mv ltee-project ltee-project-copy
cd ltee-project-copy
```

```{.bash .expect-fail}
pixi exec python scripts/first_line_absolute.py
```

```text
FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '/Users/ada/cbio7501/ltee-project/metadata/README.md'
```

The fix is a **relative** path, which works wherever the project folder is, as
long as you run scripts from the project folder:

```{.python filename="scripts/first_line.py" .write}
print(open("metadata/README.md").readline())
```

```{.bash .run}
pixi exec python scripts/first_line.py
```

Clean up and rename the folder back:

```{.bash .run}
rm scripts/first_line_absolute.py scripts/first_line.py
cd ~/cbio7501
mv ltee-project-copy ltee-project
cd ltee-project
```

::: {.callout-note}
Paths like `C:\Users\ada\Desktop\data.csv` or `/Users/ada/...` in shared code
are one of the most common reasons a project fails for someone else. In every
later lesson, run commands from the project folder and use relative paths.
:::

## Troubleshooting

| Problem | What to do |
|---------|------------|
| `pixi: command not found` | Do [lesson 00](00-setup.qmd) first, then open a new terminal. |
| `git: command not found` or "Unable to clone" | Cookiecutter downloads the template with Git. Keep `--spec git` in the command, or install Git (lesson 00). |
| `Error: "ltee-project" directory already exists` | You ran the template twice. Remove or rename the old folder, or answer with another folder name. |
| `ERROR: 'My Project' is not a good folder name` | The folder name must be lowercase with dashes, e.g. `ltee-project`. |
| The questions look stuck | Cookiecutter is waiting for your answer: type it and press Enter. |
| Windows: the files are not visible in Explorer | You are working inside WSL2: run `explorer.exe .` in the project folder. |

## Apply it to your own mini-analysis

From this lesson on you also work on a small analysis of your own (the
capstone). Generate a second project for it with the same template, from
`~/cbio7501`, with your own project name. Then, in its `README.md`, write one
paragraph: the question, the data (source, size, license) and what you expect
to produce. This is your project proposal.

## Key points

- Decide the layout before the first file arrives; use the same layout in every project.
- Raw data is read-only and downloaded by code; derived data and results are rebuilt by code.
- A template saves time, but know why each folder is there.
- Name files so they sort and can be parsed: no spaces, ISO dates, leading zeros, consistent order.
- Use paths relative to the project folder; absolute paths break on any other computer.
